def: Care that looks at the whole person: body, mind, feelings, relationships and surroundings, not just their illness.
Care planned around what the person wants, needs and values. The person helps make the decisions.
Protecting children and adults at risk from abuse, neglect and harm, and acting quickly when you are worried.
Keeping a person's private information safe. You share it only with people who need to know, usually with permission.
A person agrees to care or research after being told, in words they understand, what it involves and the risks.
Treating someone unfairly because of who they are, for example their age, disability, race, sex or religion.
A personal feature the Equality Act 2010 protects from unfair treatment, such as age, disability, race or religion.
Speaking up for a person, or helping them speak up, so their views and rights are heard.
Helping people gain more control over their own lives and choices.
Treating a person with respect so they feel valued and in control, for example by protecting their privacy.
Different organisations, such as the NHS, the council and charities, working together to support one person.
A group of professionals with different jobs, such as nurse, therapist and social worker, planning care together.
The main professional who coordinates a person's support and is their usual point of contact.
A written plan of a person's needs, goals and the support they will get. It is reviewed regularly.
Checking what could cause harm, how likely and how serious it is, and deciding how to reduce it.
Thinking carefully about what you did, how it went and what you will do differently next time.
A signed account from a supervisor or observer of what you did on placement, used as evidence.
Care given in a person's own home, for example help with washing, dressing or taking medicine.
The organisation that inspects and rates health and social care services in England and can require improvements.
An NHS organisation that plans and pays for health services for the people in its local area.
An unfair, avoidable gap in health between groups of people, for example between richer and poorer areas.
Testing people who seem healthy to find a condition early, so treatment can start sooner.
A professional's decision about which illness or condition a person has, based on symptoms, tests and examination.
Treatment and support that helps someone regain skills and independence after illness, injury or surgery.
Care for people with an illness that cannot be cured, focusing on comfort, pain relief and quality of life.
Unfair negative views that make a person feel ashamed or judged, for example about mental illness.
The close emotional bond between a baby and the person who cares for them. It affects later relationships.
A mental framework built from experience that helps a child organise and understand the world (Piaget).
How much a person values and respects themselves, and how worthy they feel.
The argument about whether development is shaped more by inherited genes (nature) or by experience and surroundings (nurture).
Explains mental illness as an inherited weakness (diathesis) combined with a stressful event that triggers it.
A group of conditions that damage the brain over time, causing memory loss, confusion and difficulty with daily life.
A sudden rise in cases of an infection in one place, for example in a nursery.
A micro-organism, such as a bacterium or virus, that can cause disease.
Actions that stop infections spreading, such as handwashing, cleaning, protective equipment and keeping ill people apart.
The body keeping its inside conditions, such as temperature and blood glucose, steady when outside conditions change.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in the body, for example amylase breaking down starch.
One version of a gene. You inherit one allele of each gene from each parent.
Taking a small sample of tissue from the body to examine under a microscope for disease.
An epidemic is a fast spread of an infectious disease in an area. A pandemic spreads across the world.
Weigh up strengths and weaknesses using evidence, then reach a judgement you can support.
Give reasons and evidence to show that a choice or decision is right or reasonable.
Break something into parts and explain how the parts connect or what they show.
Weigh up the important factors in a situation and decide which matter most.
Say how two or more things are similar and how they are different.
Look at different sides of a topic and explain how important each one is.
Give reasons: say what happens or what is true, and why.
Give a clear account of what something is like, using details.
Give the main points briefly, without lots of detail.
How far is a statement true? Give arguments on both sides, then decide how strongly you agree.
Facts, examples or information that show something is true or support your point.
A decision or opinion you reach after weighing up the evidence.
The situation around something that helps explain it, such as a person's age, home and needs.
One of the things that causes or influences a result. It is not the same as a fact.
The effect something has on a person or situation.
A weakness that makes something less useful, reliable or complete.
Suggest what should be done and give reasons why it is the best choice.
A particular way of seeing something, based on a person's experience or on a theory.
Exact and clear, not general. Name the real person, place or detail.
Closely connected to the question or case, so it helps answer it.
